answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: New enterprises lack finance, because banks will not lend to a business with no trading record or collateral. Their owners often lack experience, so they make mistakes in pricing or record keeping that can cause the business to fail.

stem: Evaluate whether governments should give grants, rather than loans, to start-ups.

points.description: Grants: no repayment, so no cash-flow burden on the new business (1)
Grants: encourage people who fear debt to start (1)
Grants: costly to taxpayers; money not recovered if businesses fail (1)
Loans: repaid and re-lent; encourage careful use of money (1)
Loans: repayments may strain cash flow in early months (1)
Justified conclusion (1)

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Grants do not have to be repaid, so new businesses avoid repayments in their difficult early months, and more people are willing to start. But grants are expensive for taxpayers, and money given to businesses that fail is lost. Loans are repaid and can be lent again, and owners tend to use borrowed money more carefully, though repayments can strain cash flow. A mix is best: small grants for training and planning, and low-interest loans with repayment holidays for equipment.

explanation: Compare cost to government with effect on start-ups and conclude.
hints: What happens to a loan when it is repaid?

stem: Sipho, 20, wants to start a mobile car-servicing business in Masvingo. He needs US\$5,400 for tools and a second-hand motorbike. He has US\$900 saved and his uncle offers US\$1,500 interest-free. A government youth fund offers loans at a low interest rate to applicants who complete a five-day business training course.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate how much Sipho would need to borrow from the youth fund.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Identify **three** types of support available to Sipho.

points.description: Own savings (1)
Family (uncle's interest-free loan) (1)
Government: low-interest loan and training (1)

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Explain **two** reasons why the youth fund requires training before lending.

points.description: Reason 1: improves business skills (1)
Developed: lower chance of failure, so loan more likely repaid (1)
Reason 2: helps applicants write a business plan / manage cash (1)
Developed: money used well, fund can lend to others (1)

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Discuss whether Sipho should accept his uncle's offer as well as the youth loan.

points.description: For: interest-free, reduces the amount borrowed at interest (1)
For: quick, flexible, no collateral (1)
Against: risk to family relationship if business fails (1)
Against: uncle may expect a say in decisions (1)
Suggests a written agreement on repayment (1)
Justified conclusion (1)

answerSpec.modelAnswer: The uncle's US\$1,500 is interest-free, so Sipho borrows less from the fund and pays less interest, and the money is available quickly without collateral. But if the business fails, Sipho may be unable to repay, which could damage the family relationship, and his uncle may expect a say in decisions. He should accept, but agree in writing when and how the money will be repaid.

explanation: Borrowing needed: 5,400 − 900 − 1,500 = US\$3,000. Combining support sources lowers cost but each has drawbacks.
hints: Subtract all the money he already has.

stem: A government plans a programme for start-ups in a region with high unemployment. It will offer cheap workspace in incubators, free advice and loan guarantees.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Identify **two** reasons why the government wants to support start-ups in this region.

points.description: Reduce unemployment / create jobs (1)
Economic growth / regional development / future tax (1)

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Explain how **two** parts of the programme help start-ups.

points.description: Incubator workspace (1)
Developed: lower start-up costs, shared equipment and mentoring (1)
Loan guarantees / advice (1)
Developed: banks lend without collateral / better plans and decisions (1)

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Evaluate whether the programme is likely to succeed in creating lasting businesses.

points.description: Strength: tackles finance and premises, two main barriers (1)
Strength: advice improves management, lowering failure rates (1)
Limitation: cannot create demand if local incomes are low (1)
Limitation: limited funds / may favour well-connected / dependency (1)
Recognises dependence on business ideas and markets (1)
Justified conclusion (1)

answerSpec.modelAnswer: The programme tackles the main barriers: finance (through guarantees) and premises (through incubators), and advice should cut early mistakes. But it cannot create customers: in a region with high unemployment, local incomes are low, so start-ups may struggle to sell. Funds may be limited and could go to the best-connected applicants. It will create lasting businesses if it also helps start-ups reach markets outside the region.

explanation: Governments support start-ups for jobs and growth; support works when it tackles real barriers and there is demand.
hints: Which barriers does each part remove?
